what_it_does: Running a large language model on a single GPU is often impossible because the model's billions of parameters do not all fit in the GPU's memory. The usual fixes — buying multiple GPUs, or shuttling data back and forth between the GPU and the main system memory over a slow PCIe connection — are either expensive or slow. LIA takes a different approach: it offloads part of the computation to the CPU, which has access to far more memory than the GPU. Modern Intel CPUs (codenamed Sapphire Rapids and Granite Rapids) include dedicated matrix-math acceleration units called AMX tiles that can perform large numerical computations at high speed, making the CPU a credible partner rather than a slow fallback. LIA also plugs in CXL memory — a relatively affordable way to attach extra memory chips to the CPU via a fast standardized link — to expand the total memory pool available for storing model parameters. The system dynamically divides each transformer layer's computation between CPU and GPU based on whether the goal is low latency or high throughput.
